Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Both sides of a fight may be in the room: no real names, no retelling, no staged apologies, and nobody owes forgiveness.

Every student in the room

Repair looks different from family to family (sometimes action, sometimes words), and making it right should never depend on money.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Open plainly: “You’ve known how to say sorry since you were little. Today is the next level.”

Slide 2 · Notes

Vote with fingers. Then ask which matters least. Expect lots of 1s and 6s. The next slide shows the answer.

Slide 3 · Notes

Compare with the room’s vote. Then ask: “Why does ‘I’m sorry’ alone feel thin?”

Slide 4 · Notes

The part people skip. Regret, explanation and a promise all helped, about equally, in the middle.

Slide 5 · Notes

If you drop one part, drop this one. Forgiveness is theirs to give when they’re ready.

Slide 6 · Notes

Ask: “Why does the first text get harder the longer you wait?” Going first feels like losing, so both people wait.

Slide 7 · Notes

Two or three sentences, using their own name in the third person. Nobody shares. Then ask by thumbs: “Did anything look different?”

Slide 8 · Notes

Cooling down can take an hour or a few days. Online: move it offline (“can we talk tomorrow?”), delete what you posted in the heat of it, and don’t screenshot and share.

Slide 9 · Notes

Read the four out loud; groups pick one. The next slide shows the one that lands. Then: say it in person or on a call if you can.

Slide 10 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 11 · Notes

Accepting again to keep the peace, or mocking him back, keeps the loop going.

Slide 12 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 13 · Notes

Both are waiting for the other. Skip recruiting teammates. Things you skip repairing tend to come back bigger.

Slide 14 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 15 · Notes

They may not have known how it landed, so let them answer. You can accept an apology and still need time.

Slide 16 · Notes

Private, on the back of your card: “How does your family usually make things right?” A friend’s apology may come in a form you weren’t looking for. Nobody shares.

Slide 17 · Notes

Turn and talk. Then ask: “Where else in your life does this show up?” Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 18 · Notes

Students draft on their card, real or practice, and keep it. Share the take-home link after.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can name which parts of an apology matter most (taking responsibility, then an offer to fix it), explain why sorry is hard to say, use the repair sequence on a real or practice conflict, and know their options when they're the one who got hurt. Nobody retells a real fight in class.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 7 minGuess the ranking, then the answers one per slide
  2. 5 minWhy sorry is so hard
  3. 4 minStep back (private, nobody shares)
  4. 5 minThe repair sequence
  5. 10 minWhich apology lands? Three moments, one per slide
  6. 6 minIf you got hurt; repair looks different in every family
  7. 3 minWhere else does this show up? and draft it messy

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Guess the ranking and the three answers, the repair sequence, the Mia moment, and draft it messy. Share the take-home link afterward.

Before you teach
Both sides of a fight may be in the room.

9th grade conflicts often run through one advisory or one team. No real names, no retelling current fights, no "who was wrong" discussions. The reflections are private and stay on cards that go home.

Don't stage apologies in class.

If a conflict between students is live, handle it outside the lesson with a counselor or dean. A lesson on repair isn't the place to make anyone say sorry in front of peers.

Hurt, then sorry, again and again, is a pattern.

If a student describes someone who keeps hurting them and apologizing, at school, in a dating relationship, or at home, thank them and connect them with a counselor that day. Don't problem-solve it in front of the class.

Nobody owes forgiveness.

Students who were hurt can accept an apology and still need time to trust, or decline one that comes with no change. Avoid language that pressures the hurt person to "just move on."

Some situations need an adult more than an apology.

Threats to anyone, a fight turning into a pile-on online or at school, or something that made a student feel unsafe. Say this plainly near the end, and know who you'd walk a student to.

Screenshots of fights come up.

Students may bring up a group chat fight everyone saw. Keep it general. If someone's private messages or photos are being passed around, that's a counselor conversation that day.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Repair looks different from family to family.

Some families expect a direct "I was wrong." Others repair through action: showing up, doing a favor, cooking for someone, acting normal again. Some rarely say sorry out loud. Present each as real repair and ask about students' own families privately.

The people you can't walk away from vary.

For some students it's a sibling, a step-sibling, a cousin they share a room with, or a parent in one of two homes. In some families an older relative steps in to settle things. Use "someone you live with" so every household fits.

Apologizing in a second language.

Getting the words exactly right is harder in a language you're still learning, and text strips out tone. Students who are new to English can apologize in person, by action, or in writing they've had time to check. The Andre card (mocking an accent) names a hurt these students know.

Neurodivergent students may need a script and time.

Cooling down can take longer, and reading tone over text is harder for some students. The repair sequence works as a script. Eye contact isn't required for an apology to count, and a written apology can be the right choice.

Faith can be a resource here.

Some students' traditions have practices of confession, forgiveness, or making amends; others have none. Let "how does your family or tradition make things right?" cover both without assuming either.

Making it right shouldn't depend on money.

"Paying for what broke" is one kind of repair offer. Deleting a post, telling the group it was your fault, fixing or replacing something with time or effort all count. Keep the examples free.

What the research says

755 people rated apologies built from six possible parts. Apologies with more parts worked better, but the parts weren't equal. The studies were with adults.

Lewicki, Polin and Lount, Negotiation and Conflict Management Research, 2016 (Ohio State)

Taking responsibility mattered most, then an offer of repair. Regret, explanation, and a promise to change were in the middle. Asking for forgiveness mattered least.

Lewicki, Polin and Lount, 2016

Across four studies, people who believe personality can change were more likely to take responsibility after hurting someone.

Schumann and Dweck, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2014

People who wrote a message refusing to apologize felt more powerful and had higher self-esteem afterward than people who didn't.

Okimoto, Wenzel and Hedrick, European Journal of Social Psychology, 2013

People reasoned more wisely about a friend's relationship conflict than their own: considering other viewpoints, admitting what they didn't know, looking for compromise.

Grossmann and Kross, Psychological Science, 2014

When people thought about their own conflict from a distance, for example in the third person, the gap disappeared, in younger and older adults alike.

Grossmann and Kross, Psychological Science, 2014
